cards.title: Polynomial-time weighted falsifiability of unambiguous DNFs
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the total binary input length, that solves the following problem? The input consists of an unambiguous DNF $F=\bigvee_{j=1}^{m}T_j$ over n Boolean variables, nonnegative integer weights w_1,...,w_n encoded in binary, and an integer threshold t encoded in binary. Decide whether there exists $a\in\{0,1\}^n$ such that $F(a)=0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i a_i\ge t$. Each T_j is an explicitly listed conjunction of literals. Unambiguous means that no assignment satisfies two distinct terms simultaneously.
cards.definitions: A literal is either x_i or its negation. A term is true exactly when all its literals are true; the DNF is true when at least one term is true. Contradictory terms can be discarded. For the remaining terms, unambiguity is equivalent to every pair containing opposite literals on some variable, so this promise is itself checkable in polynomial time. Weights are exact integers, with no rounding. The running time must depend polynomially on their bit lengths rather than on their numerical sum. The threshold uses at least, not exactly; a strict-threshold formulation is equivalent by shifting the integer threshold by one. The output is a yes/no answer. A tautology has no falsifying assignment and always gives no, regardless of the threshold.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all such inputs, or prove that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-hardness proof would provide a negative answer conditional on P differing from NP; its assumption must be stated. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a method only for unweighted assignments, or hardness after changing the comparison to exact equality does not settle the specified question.
cards.why: The problem separates easy counting from optimization on the complement of a simple disjoint representation. It tests whether unambiguity retains its algorithmic value when a compactly encoded additive objective is introduced, and it bears on the power of knowledge-compilation representations under negation.

importance.reason: A focused but structural tractability question connecting unambiguous representations, binary-weight optimization, and complementation. It has a clear gap between polynomial unweighted methods and an unresolved weighted case.

progress.text: Monet formulates the binary-weight optimization problem and records NP membership of its decision version, polynomial-time weighted satisfaction, and a pseudopolynomial dynamic program for falsification.
The Dagstuhl seminar on database representation and provenance presents this exact question by linking to Monet’s formulation. The catalogue’s separate TCS-0485 record comes from that link.

Amarilli’s maintained list still asks for a polynomial-time weighted-falsifiability algorithm and discusses its connection to complementation of d-DNNFs. Monet’s original question has no posted answer at this check.

context_blocks.text: Unambiguity makes the satisfying regions disjoint. This is useful for counting: after fixing the literals of one consistent term, every remaining variable is free, and the term’s satisfying assignments can be counted directly. Summing across terms gives the total without any inclusion-exclusion correction. Subtracting that count from 2^n decides whether a falsifying assignment exists at all.

The weighted version asks where the complement lies relative to an additive score. Knowing how many points lie outside the DNF does not reveal whether even one of them has a large score. For example, take F=(x AND y) OR ((NOT x) AND z), whose two terms are incompatible. With weights 8, 3, and 5, the assignment (1,0,1) falsifies F and has score 13. The all-ones assignment has larger score 16 but satisfies F, so unconstrained maximization does not answer the question.

There is an important asymmetry between maximizing over satisfying and falsifying assignments. To maximize over satisfying assignments, optimize each term separately by setting every unrestricted positive-weight variable to one, then take the best result. To falsify the DNF, every term must fail at once, and choices made to destroy one term can interact with all the others.

Dynamic programming over achievable scores gives a pseudopolynomial algorithm; it becomes polynomial when weights are unary. The missing guarantee is polynomial dependence on binary descriptions of potentially large weights. Amarilli also explains a connection to complementing compiled Boolean representations: efficient complementation into a representation supporting weighted maximization would give an algorithm, while suitable hardness would obstruct that route.

cards.definitions: A Boolean function family is f=(fₙ:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1})_{n≥1}. A linear decision list consists of s ordered pairs (qᵢ,bᵢ) and a default bit b_{s+1}. On input x, it returns bᵢ at the first i for which qᵢ(x)=1, or the default if all tests fail. Each query is qᵢ(x)=1 iff wᵢ,₀+∑_{j=1}^n wᵢ,ⱼxⱼ>0, with integer weights wᵢ,ⱼ, including the offset wᵢ,₀. Allowing a test for qᵢ(x)=0 is equivalent on integer-valued sums to another query of this form. Size is the number s of queries; weights’ bit lengths are not charged as extra queries. LDL consists of all families admitting, for some fixed constants c,C>0, lists of size at most C(n+1)^c at every n, with no bound on integer weights. LDL_polywt requires in addition constants b,B>0 such that every weight in every list has absolute value at most B(n+1)^b. Constants are uniform across input lengths and queries, but may depend on the family. Neither class requires an algorithm generating the lists. Polynomial magnitude is stronger than polynomial bit length: a weight 2ⁿ has n+1 bits but is not polynomially bounded in magnitude. There is no additional bound on the number of changes in the output sequence (b₁,…,b_{s+1}); it may grow as large as the list length. Proper inclusion means that some family lies in LDL but not LDL_polywt. Equivalently, for that family, every pair of fixed polynomial size and weight bounds fails at some input lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some family has polynomial-size unrestricted-weight lists but has no family of polynomial-size, polynomial-magnitude-weight lists, or prove LDL_polywt=LDL by establishing such bounded-weight representations for every LDL family. A lower bound that applies only while alternation depth is restricted does not settle this target.

context_blocks.title: A list stops at its first successful test
context_blocks.text: A threshold test can compare a weighted sum of input bits with a threshold. A decision list checks several such conditions in order, and the first success chooses the output. This model permits branching by the order of tests, even though it is simpler than an arbitrary decision tree.

context_blocks.title: Large numbers and more tests may compensate for each other
context_blocks.text: An individual threshold can use exponentially large integer weights. The question asks whether polynomially many tests with polynomially bounded weights can always reproduce the behavior of a polynomial-size list that uses those large numbers. Merely proving that one threshold requires large weights is insufficient.

context_blocks.title: Why unrestricted alternation matters
context_blocks.text: A list returning 0,1,0,1 in successive branches switches output value several times. The paper proves weight-sensitive separations under a bound on such alternation. Once that restriction is removed, additional changes in output value may increase the power of bounded-weight lists.

context_blocks.title: The known comparison stops short of the full classes
context_blocks.text: For the greater-than function, the paper gives an exponential-in-n/k lower bound for bounded-weight lists at bounded alternation parameter k, while an unrestricted-weight threshold suffices. This does not exclude polynomial-size bounded-weight lists with much larger alternation, so the full-class inclusion remains the distinct question.

cards.title: Decision-tree reductions from Nephew to Lossy-Code
cards.formal: Prove or refute the source’s concrete conjecture Nephew ≰dt Lossy-Code. In Nephew, given oracle access to two total functions f,g:V→V on an arbitrary finite nonempty set V, output v∈V such that f(f(g(v)))≠f(v) or f(g(v))=v. The relation ≼dt is the deterministic polylogarithmic-complexity reduction defined below; replacing it with randomized or white-box reductions changes the question.
cards.why: Would give a structurally motivated total zero-error randomized search problem beyond the class captured by lossy compression. It tests whether a prominent organizing principle for total search captures Nephew’s finite combinatorial obstruction.

references.title: Total Search Problems in ZPP
references.authors: Fleming, Noah; Grosser, Stefan; Jain, Siddhartha; Li, Jiawei; Ren, Hanlin; Shirley, Morgan; Yuan, Weiqiang
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 21; PDF page 21

cards.definitions: Encode V by integer labels and encode the two function tables in binary. Let N=|V| and let n denote the total table bit length, Θ(N log(N+1)); the tables are accessed through queries, not supplied for free as readable circuit descriptions. A function-value query can be simulated by O(log(N+1)) bit queries, so either interface gives the same polylogarithmic scale. Lossy-Code_{M→2M} supplies oracle functions e:[M]→[2M] and d:[2M]→[M] and asks for z∈[2M] with e(d(z))≠z. The letters e,d denote expansion and compression; they are unrelated to Nephew’s f,g. For search relations R on n input bits and S on m input bits, an S-formulation of R has a deterministic decision tree F_i computing each target bit i from the source input x, and, for every possible target solution o, a decision tree G_o decoding a source output. It must satisfy (F(x),o)∈S⇒(x,G_o(x))∈R for every x and every valid target solution o. If d_* is the maximum depth of these trees, the reduction’s complexity is log m+d_*. R≼dt S means that this is at most (log(n+2))^{O(1)} for the entire family, with a fixed exponent. The reduction is nonuniform in input length and may describe a target table of quasipolynomial or larger-than-polynomial size as long as log m is polylogarithmic; it cannot inspect that whole table. TFZPPdt consists of total search families with polylogarithmic verification-query complexity and randomized polylogarithmic-depth query algorithms which never return an invalid solution, may return failure, and fail with probability at most 1/3 on each input.
cards.answer_criterion: Show that no family of Lossy-Code formulations of Nephew has complexity bounded by any fixed power of log n; or refute the candidate by giving such a formulation and proving that every target solution decodes correctly. A failure of a particular attempted reduction is not a separation. An efficient reduction would refute the Nephew candidate without settling whether some other natural TFZPPdt problem lies outside LOSSY.

cards.title: Randomized evidence versus certain proofs
cards.formal: Are there properties of growing families of finite mathematical objects that can be certified efficiently with arbitrarily high probabilistic confidence, yet have no comparably short certain proofs? The source poses this as a broad question about mathematical evidence; an object encoding, randomized guarantee and proof system must be fixed before it defines a separation to prove.
cards.why: Asks how probabilistic computational evidence compares with certain verification of finite mathematical facts. Its significance depends on distinguishing practical reproducibility, derandomization and proof complexity rather than merging them into one undefined obstacle.
cards.status_note: Full source discussion, primality comparison and subsequent searches checked through 11 September 2026. The source does not formulate one proof system or asymptotic separation, so its broad question cannot receive a single verified open/closed disposition.

progress.text: The deterministic polynomial-time primality theorem rules out primality as an asymptotic example of the proposed randomized-versus-deterministic separation.
The FUN paper raises the broad evidence-versus-proof question in its discussion of reproducible probabilistic diameter bounds.

cards.definitions: For a complexity-theoretic formulation, encode an object by a binary string x of length n and represent the property by a language L. A bounded-error randomized polynomial-time decider gives the correct membership answer with probability at least 2/3 on every input; independent repetition can reduce this error to δ with O(log(1/δ)) repetitions. A deterministic polynomial-time decider instead always gives the correct answer. A different notion is a polynomially checkable certificate: a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and polynomial p satisfy x∈L iff there exists a string π of length at most p(n) with V(x,π)=1. This asks for certificate existence and efficient checking, not for efficiently finding the certificate. A proof-length question in a particular formal calculus additionally fixes that calculus, its axioms and proof encoding. A bound on the probability that an experiment issues a false certificate is a sampling guarantee; it is not automatically a posterior probability that a fixed mathematical statement is false. For one fixed finite object, asymptotic proof-length claims require a growing parameter or a family, since a single statement can be treated as a constant-size instance.
cards.answer_criterion: Select one precise family, evidence protocol, resource scale and sound proof notion, then prove or refute the resulting separation. A large experiment, a small p-value, practical difficulty finding a proof, or a lower bound only for one proof method does not by itself establish absence of all short certificates in a broader model.

references.title: Total NP Search Problems with Abundant Solutions
references.authors: Li, Jiawei
references.locator: Open Problem 2; PDF page 19

cards.definitions: Take n≥4, vertex set {0,1}^n and one input bit for each unordered pair of distinct vertices; let N=binom(2^n,2) be the number of these bits. A solution lists ⌊n/2⌋ distinct vertices and identifies whether all pairs are edges or all are nonedges. Each solution can be verified with O(n²)=poly(log N) queries. A black-box TFNP problem is a family R_N⊆{0,1}^N×O_N, with finite solution sets O_N, total on every input, and with a decision tree of depth poly(log N) verifying each proposed solution. A partial input a∈{0,1,*}^N is witnessing if some one output o is valid for every complete input extending a. A function h(N) is negligible in log N when, for every constant c>0, h(N)≤(log N)^{-c} for all sufficiently large N. A problem is robust if for every such nonnegative h, all sufficiently large N have the property that every partial input fixing at least (1−h(N))N bits is witnessing. A deterministic decision-tree many-one reduction R_N→Q_M has one depth-poly(log N) tree computing each target input bit and, for every target solution o, one such tree decoding a source solution; log M is poly(log N). For every source input x and every valid target solution o of the constructed target, decoding must give a valid source solution. No uniform circuit-construction condition is imposed on these decision trees. TFAP^dt consists precisely of problems reducible in this sense to a robust black-box TFNP problem. The source’s circuit-input TFAP definition assigns membership through this oracle counterpart: an explicit succinct adjacency circuit does not authorize a stronger, arbitrary white-box reduction. The floor fixes the harmless integer convention for the source’s n/2 notation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a low-depth decision-tree many-one reduction from this Ramsey search family to a robust total search family, with the required target-size bound and correctness for every target solution, or prove that no such reduction exists. Showing merely that every graph has many Ramsey sets, or proving membership for the smaller n/10 target, does not resolve this membership question.

cards.definitions: A total NP search problem is a polynomial-time decidable relation R(a,z) with polynomially bounded witnesses z and at least one witness for every input a. A reduction R≤S consists of deterministic polynomial-time maps F and G such that every S-witness w for F(a) gives an R-witness G(a,w); running times are polynomial in the explicit input lengths. For EndOfPotentialLine, an instance consists of circuits P,S:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1}ⁿ and V:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,…,2ᵐ−1}, for n,m≥1, with P(0ⁿ)=0ⁿ, S(0ⁿ)≠0ⁿ and V(0ⁿ)=0. Potentials are m-bit nonnegative integers. A valid answer is a vertex x satisfying at least one of: (a) P(S(x))≠x; (b) x≠0ⁿ and S(P(x))≠x; (c) x≠S(x), P(S(x))=x and V(S(x))≤V(x). UniqueEOPL has the same instances and accepts all these answers, and additionally accepts two vertices x≠y with x≠S(x), y≠S(y), and either V(x)=V(y) or V(x)<V(y)<V(S(x)). Thus uniqueness is enforced by additional verifiable witnesses, not assumed as an unverifiable promise. Circuits are finite acyclic AND/OR/NOT circuits with their complete gate lists as input; size includes all gates, wires, input and output labels. The displayed restrictions at 0ⁿ are directly checkable; malformed encodings or failed restrictions may be assigned a distinguished trivial answer. EOPL and UEOPL consist of all total NP search problems reducible to their respective canonical problems by the reductions just defined. In particular UEOPL⊆EOPL, since an EndOfPotentialLine answer is always also a UniqueEOPL answer.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove equality by a polynomial-time reduction from EndOfPotentialLine to UniqueEOPL, valid for every output that the target relation permits, or prove that no such reduction exists. A separation limited to oracle queries or decision trees does not establish inequality of the ordinary circuit-defined classes.

If a d-local Boolean map on independent uniform input bits has output distribution X at total variation distance at most ε from a distribution uniform on a nonempty union of Hamming-weight layers in {0,1}ⁿ, then X is within Cε of one of the six distributions defined below.
cards.why: Classifies the ability of constant-locality classical circuits to generate uniform symmetric distributions, including approximate generation rather than only exact sampling.
cards.status_note: Resolved by Kane, Ostuni and Wu, published at STOC 2025. The complete theorem, locality and distance conventions, absolute constant, threshold dependence and six distributions were checked against arXiv v2. This is published-theorem/model verification, not independent proof verification.

cards.definitions: For m,n≥1, a map f:{0,1}ᵐ→{0,1}ⁿ is d-local if each output coordinate depends on at most d input coordinates; the chosen inputs may differ between outputs and may be shared. The input Uₘ is uniform on {0,1}ᵐ, and X is the law of f(Uₘ). There is no bound on m and no algorithmic uniformity requirement across n. For nonempty S⊆{0,…,n}, let U_Sⁿ be uniform on all strings x∈{0,1}ⁿ with |x|=Σⱼxⱼ∈S: every such string, rather than every allowed weight, has the same probability. For distributions P,Q on {0,1}ⁿ, TV(P,Q)=½Σₓ|P(x)−Q(x)|. The six comparison distributions are: a point mass at 0ⁿ; a point mass at 1ⁿ; equal mass on 0ⁿ and 1ⁿ; uniform on all even-weight strings; uniform on all odd-weight strings; and uniform on the entire cube. The quantifiers in the historical claim are ∃C>0 ∀d≥0 ∀ε∈(0,1) ∃n₀(d,ε) ∀n≥n₀ ∀m≥1 ∀d-local f ∀nonempty S: TV(f(Uₘ),U_Sⁿ)≤ε implies min_D TV(f(Uₘ),D)≤Cε, where D ranges over those six distributions. The result actually allows the threshold n₀ to depend only on d. No symmetry of f or of its output distribution is assumed.
cards.answer_criterion: The affirmative resolution is Theorem 4.1 of Kane, Ostuni and Wu, which proves the stated robust six-distribution classification, with an absolute multiplicative constant. Theorem 1.2 explicitly identifies this as the resolution of the Filmus–Leigh–Riazanov–Sokolov conjecture.

cards.title: Necessary logarithmic amplification when composing XOR with a total function
cards.formal: Historical existence question, resolved affirmatively: are there total nonconstant Boolean functions g for which the randomized query cost of XOR of n independent input blocks is Ω(n log n · R(g))? In explicit asymptotic terms, seek an absolute c>0 and, for arbitrarily large n, an input length m=m(n) and total nonconstant gₙ:{0,1}ᵐ→{0,1} with R(XORₙ∘gₙⁿ)≥c n log₂ n R(gₙ). The source also permits the analogous majority lower bound as an alternative affirmative answer. Corollary 1.3 of the 2023 paper establishes the XOR alternative. The inner function and its input length may grow with n; the claim is not about a single fixed finite truth table for unbounded n.
cards.why: Shows that error reduction can impose a genuine logarithmic cost in composing randomized computations even when every inner input is valid.
cards.status_note: Matched Open Question 12, including its truncated majority alternative, to the explicit total-function Corollary 1.3. Read the worst-case/expected definitions and the supporting 2019 theorem’s parameter regime. Verified the final 2023 publication and searched subsequent XOR literature. No independent proof audit is claimed, and no majority theorem is inferred.

references.title: When Is Amplification Necessary for Composition in Randomized Query Complexity?
references.authors: Ben-David, Shalev; Göös, Mika; Kothari, Robin; Watson, Thomas
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 13; PDF page 13

cards.definitions: For input blocks x¹,…,xⁿ∈{0,1}ᵐ, (XORₙ∘gⁿ)(x¹,…,xⁿ)=g(x¹)⊕⋯⊕g(xⁿ), where ⊕ is addition modulo two. The blocks are separate parts of an arbitrary worst-case input; they are not promised to be randomly sampled. A randomized decision tree chooses which input bit to read next from previously read bits and internal random coins. Each bit read costs one query. R(h) is the smallest q for which such an algorithm always makes at most q queries, for every input and every coin outcome, and outputs h correctly with probability at least 2/3 on every input. There is no abort outcome and no postselection. Internal computation and the description of h are free; this is decision-tree complexity, denoted BPP(h) in the source, not the uniform time class BPP. Total means g is defined on all 2ᵐ inputs. The comparison uses the optimal cost of one copy, not the cost of a particular algorithm for g. In the source’s alternative, MAJₙ outputs one when at least n/2 of its input bits are one, including a tie. The later theorem also uses R̄δ(h): the minimum, over algorithms with error at most δ on every input, of the maximum over inputs of their expected query count. R̄ and R are distinct cost conventions; the stated resolved target uses R on both sides.
cards.answer_criterion: An unbounded family satisfying the displayed worst-case, 1/3-error lower bound for XOR answers the source question affirmatively; the generic O(n log n R(g)) upper bound makes the dependence tight up to constants. A majority family with the same lower bound would also answer the original disjunction, but is unnecessary once XOR is established. A promise function, noisy input oracle or postselection lower bound alone would not meet the total-function target.

cards.definitions: The input is a directed graph G=(V,E), with V=[n], n≥2, no loops or parallel arcs, and distinguished s≠t. Both opposite arcs between two vertices are allowed. The graph is unweighted; every arc has length one. A simple s-to-t path is a sequence v₀=s,v₁,…,v_ℓ=t of pairwise distinct vertices with (v_{j−1},v_j)∈E for 1≤j≤ℓ, and its length is ℓ. If t is reachable from s, dist_G(s,t) is the minimum length of such a path. If t is unreachable, the instance is a no-instance. The input lists all vertices and arcs using binary vertex labels; N is the full encoding length. Polynomial time means one deterministic multitape Turing machine that decides every instance in at most C(N+1)^a steps for absolute constants C,a. NP-completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions; in particular, a hardness proof can give a map from Boolean satisfiability instances to these graph instances that preserves yes/no answers. The decision problem is in NP: an at-most-n-vertex path is a polynomial-size certificate, and reachability distance and the path conditions can be checked in polynomial time. No planarity, acyclicity, connectivity or uniqueness of shortest paths is promised.
cards.answer_criterion: Determine the problem’s complexity in the stated unrestricted directed, unweighted model. A deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm establishes tractability; a polynomial-time many-one reduction from SAT establishes NP-completeness, since membership in NP is known. The latter excludes a polynomial-time algorithm under P≠NP. The question does not assume a P/NP-complete dichotomy in advance; any different established classification must explain the remaining boundary. Bounds only for planar graphs, or hardness when k is variable, do not classify the fixed k=1 problem.

context_blocks.title: Another shortest path is not enough
context_blocks.text: The question asks for strictly greater length. A graph may have many different shortest s-to-t paths and still have no simple path longer than them. Finding a second distinct path therefore does not by itself decide the problem.

context_blocks.title: Repeated vertices change the task

context_blocks.title: A minimal increase can still hide global structure
context_blocks.text: Shortest paths are efficiently computable, but deciding whether their length can be exceeded by a simple path constrains which vertices can be reused. Here even one additional edge is the unresolved threshold.

cards.definitions: Terms are generated by variables from a countably infinite set, application MN and abstraction λx.M, modulo renaming bound variables. Beta-convertibility is the least equivalence relation closed under application and abstraction containing (λx.M)N=M[N/x], with capture-avoiding substitution. A directed set is nonempty and every two of its elements have an upper bound in the set. D is a set with a partial order, a least element, and a supremum for every directed subset. Scott-continuous means monotone and preserving directed suprema. [D→D] consists of all Scott-continuous functions, ordered pointwise. An environment ρ assigns an element of D to each variable. Interpret x as ρ(x), MN as F(⟦M⟧ρ)(⟦N⟧ρ), and λx.M as L(d↦⟦M⟧(ρ[x:=d])). The desired condition is ∀M,N: (∀ρ, ⟦M⟧ρ=⟦N⟧ρ) ⇔ M=βN. Models need not be countable, algebraic, effectively presented or extensional; in particular L∘F=id is not required. These are set-based directed-complete orders and all their continuous maps, without a restriction to graph models.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that a pointed dcpo and continuous retraction F,L satisfying the stated exact-theory condition exist, or prove that none exist. A negative answer must cover all such dcpos, without assuming an effective presentation, algebraicity or extensionality.

sentences: Scott's continuous semantics interprets untyped lambda terms using mathematical domains and continuous functions.
The project asks whether some model identifies exactly the pairs of terms related by beta-conversion.
Beta-conversion expresses equality generated by applying functions to arguments and substituting those arguments into their bodies.
Many semantic constructions validate additional equations, so soundness for beta-reduction alone does not answer the question.

context_blocks.text: The untyped lambda calculus describes functions using variables, application and abstraction. Beta-reduction substitutes an argument into a function body. A denotational model assigns mathematical meanings to terms and makes every beta-conversion valid. The question asks whether continuity can coexist with complete precision: no two terms should become equal in the model unless beta-conversion already equates them.

In domain semantics, an order represents increasing information and a directed supremum combines compatible approximations. Scott continuity requires functions to preserve these suprema. The map L represents each continuous self-map by an element of D, and F turns an element back into its associated self-map. The equation F∘L=id ensures that interpreting function application recovers the represented function. This makes beta-reduction sound.

Representability is a semantic condition. The element representing a continuous function need not be denoted by any finite lambda term. Requiring every continuous function to have a finite program would change the question. The model need not have computable elements, a computable ordering or a computable interpretation algorithm.

Extensional equality makes an additional identification. If x is not free in f, eta-conversion equates λx.f x with f, although these terms need not be beta-convertible. Imposing L∘F=id would validate this extra equality. This card therefore requires only the retraction in the other direction and keeps the beta-eta version as a separate target.

Quotienting syntax by beta-conversion gives a term model with exactly the desired equality. It does not automatically provide a pointed dcpo representing all continuous self-maps. The issue is whether the exact syntactic theory can be realized in this particular semantic setting.

Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra prove that the effective models defined in their paper cannot have theory exactly λβ or λβη. They also prove non-enumerability of the order theory, which records inequalities between denotations. Equational theory records equalities instead. A theorem restricted to effective models, or to order rather than equality, cannot be generalized silently to arbitrary dcpos.

Divergent terms reveal another source of extra equations. A term is unsolvable when no finite reduction exposes a head normal form: an outer variable applied to arguments after any leading abstractions. A sensible model equates all unsolvable closed terms. This is stronger than beta-conversion, which distinguishes some of them. The 2025 filter-model paper studies when unsolvables receive nontrivial interpretations and which type-theoretic conditions govern that behavior.

Lambda Galore, published in 2026, constructs sensible filter models representing all continuous functions whose theories do not contain the full Böhm-tree theory. It separates two semantic properties and resolves a different question about models. Sensibility still identifies unsolvables, so these constructions do not realize exactly λβ. Continuous representability alone does not make their equational theory the one requested here.

cards.formal: For every pure type system (S,A,R) defined below, does weak normalization of every typable term imply strong normalization of every typable term?
cards.why: Normalization connects computation with the metatheory of typed proofs. This conjecture asks whether the pure-type-system rules turn the existence of a terminating computation for every typable term into termination under every reduction order.
cards.status_note: The primary statement and Mull’s 2023 paper leave the unrestricted conjecture open. A later-result and author-publication search on 11 September 2026 found no general proof or counterexample. The positive theorems impose additional PTS structure.

cards.definitions: S is a set of sorts, A⊆S×S is a set of axioms, and R⊆S×S×S is a set of product rules. Terms are finite expressions t ::= x | s | t u | λx:B.t | Πx:B.C, with s∈S and variables from a countably infinite set, modulo renaming bound variables. A context is a finite sequence of declarations of distinct variables. Typing is the least relation Γ⊢t:B generated by the following rules. Axiom: ∅⊢s:t when (s,t)∈A. Start: Γ,x:B⊢x:B when Γ⊢B:s and x is fresh. Weakening: Γ,x:C⊢t:B when Γ⊢t:B, Γ⊢C:s and x is fresh. Product: Γ⊢Πx:B.C:s₃ when Γ⊢B:s₁, Γ,x:B⊢C:s₂ and (s₁,s₂,s₃)∈R. Abstraction: Γ⊢λx:B.t:Πx:B.C when Γ,x:B⊢t:C and Γ⊢Πx:B.C:s for a sort s. Application: Γ⊢t u:C[u/x] when Γ⊢t:Πx:B.C and Γ⊢u:B. Conversion: Γ⊢t:C when Γ⊢t:B, Γ⊢C:s and B=βC. All substitutions avoid capture. A beta step contracts (λx:B.t)u to t[u/x] at any subterm, including inside annotations and product types. =β is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of those steps. A term is typable if Γ⊢t:B for some finite Γ,B. Weak normalization means that each typable term has some finite beta-reduction sequence ending in a term with no beta redex. Strong normalization means that no typable term starts an infinite beta-reduction sequence. Both predicates quantify over open as well as closed terms and over all their reduction choices. The sets S,A,R need not be finite, decidable or functional.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every pure type system in which all typable terms are weakly beta-normalizing is strongly beta-normalizing, or exhibit a pure type system that is weakly normalizing for every typable term but has a typable term admitting an infinite beta-reduction sequence.

context_blocks.text: A term can contain several reducible applications, so computation involves choices. Weak normalization says that some sequence reaches a normal form. Strong normalization says that every sequence of beta-reductions terminates. The conjecture asks whether these two system-wide properties coincide for all pure type systems, a common framework for typed lambda calculi.

The distinction is real for untyped terms. Let Ω=(λz.zz)(λz.zz). The term (λx.y)Ω reduces to y in one step if the outer application is chosen, but it can also reduce Ω forever. Thus it is weakly but not strongly normalizing. This only illustrates the distinction: a counterexample to the conjecture needs a pure type system whose entire collection of typable terms is weakly normalizing.

A pure type system specifies which sorts classify other sorts and which dependent function types may be formed, through its sets A and R. The common typing rules generate the resulting calculus. Familiar simply typed, polymorphic and dependent systems fit the framework, but the conjecture also covers unusual specifications, beyond established proof languages.

The global hypothesis concerns every typable term. Confluence cannot replace it: confluence says that two finite reductions can be joined, making normal forms unique when they exist. It does not prevent an infinite path from coexisting with a terminating path. The untyped example already separates these ideas.

Reduction here includes type annotations and components of dependent products. Termination of an implementation’s selected evaluation strategy therefore differs from strong normalization of the calculus. Results after erasing annotations, or for closed programs only, have a different scope from the property of every annotated typable term in every context.

Sørensen’s 1997 work proves the implication for specified classes of typed calculi. Barthe, Hatcliff and Sørensen extend it to a class of non-dependent pure type systems in 2001. Their structural hypotheses are substantive: the theorem does not claim to cover every non-dependent specification, let alone every dependent one. The TLCA list records these as partial results.

Mull’s TYPES 2022 paper, published in 2023, enlarges the known class using a translation preserving typability and infinite reduction paths while removing certain sorts and rules. The theorem includes some systems with dependent rules that earlier results did not cover. The author explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture; the translation’s structural hypotheses cannot be omitted.

A universal implication would connect the existence of normal forms with complete freedom of reduction order throughout this family of type theories. A counterexample would identify a system in which every term can finish, yet some legal choices continue forever. Either outcome would sharpen normalization arguments in proof checking and the metatheory of dependent types.

cards.definitions: In round i≥1, Timer chooses a_i∈T and a nonnegative rational delay τ_i; after observing this move, Monitor chooses b_i∈M. Put t_i=∑_{j≤i}τ_j. The resulting infinite timed word is ((a_i,b_i),t_i)_{i≥1}. Timestamps may be equal or bounded above: no non-Zeno requirement is imposed. A has finitely many locations, sets of initial and accepting locations, one clock x initially zero, and finitely many transitions (ℓ,(a,b),g,Y,ℓ′), where g is a finite conjunction of x⋈c tests with ⋈∈{<,≤,=,≥,>} and c a nonnegative integer, and Y either resets x to zero or leaves it unchanged. In the ordinary model, delay τ adds τ to the clock before checking g and applying the optional reset. In the 1-resetting extension, the value checked is frac(x+τ), its fractional part; that value is retained unless the transition resets it. A word belongs to L(A) iff some run visits accepting locations infinitely often. Neither player controls this accepting-run existential quantifier. The designated owner wins exactly words in L(A), and the other player wins its complement. A Timer strategy maps finite Monitor histories to the next pair (a,τ); a Monitor strategy maps nonempty histories of Timer’s letters and timestamps to the next b. Each player can reconstruct its own past moves from its strategy. A strategy wins if every opposing response sequence yields a winning word. Determinacy requires the existence of one such strategy; a finite-state controller or synthesis algorithm is an additional requirement.

cards.definitions: Types are finite expressions generated from a countable supply of type variables by A ::= X | A→A | ∀X.A, modulo renaming bound variables. A[B/X] replaces the free occurrences of X in A by B, renaming bound variables to avoid capture. Free type variables are allowed. Church-style F_at terms are variables, typed lambda abstractions, applications, type abstractions ΛX.t, and type applications t[Y], where Y must be a type variable. In a finite context Γ assigning types to distinct term variables, the rules are: a declared variable has its assigned type; Γ,x:C ⊢ t:D yields Γ ⊢ λx:C.t:C→D; Γ ⊢ t:C→D and Γ ⊢ u:C yield Γ ⊢ tu:D; Γ ⊢ t:C yields Γ ⊢ ΛY.t:∀Y.C when Y is not free in any type of Γ; Γ ⊢ t:∀Y.C yields Γ ⊢ t[Z]:C[Z/Y] for a type variable Z. Context assumptions may be reused or left unused. Full System F instead allows any type as the last rule’s witness. Instantiation overflow requires the existence of an atomic-typed term for every B, with the term permitted to depend on A, X and B. It does not require the same term for all B, a resource bound on producing it, or equality to full instantiation under beta-eta conversion. A simple type is one with no quantifier anywhere in its body.

cards.title: Wait-free exact FIFO queues in Common₂
cards.formal: For every fixed number n≥2 of asynchronous processes, is there a deterministic wait-free linearizable implementation of an initially empty, unbounded FIFO queue using only atomic read/write registers and atomic Test&Set bits? Every process may perform both Enqueue and Dequeue, repeatedly and in any order. The implementation must satisfy exact FIFO semantics in every execution, including executions with arbitrary delays and crashes. This is the source’s Common₂ question; “some objects with consensus number two” is not a free choice of base types that could include the desired queue itself.
cards.why: Would determine whether the familiar consensus-number-two primitives suffice for an exact queue with individual progress guarantees, clarifying the limitations of the consensus hierarchy as a guide to object implementation.

cards.definitions: There are n sequential processes with distinct identifiers 1,…,n. Each invokes a new high-level operation only after its previous one returns. The scheduler interleaves atomic shared-memory steps arbitrarily; a process may stop forever at any point. A register stores a finite value and supports atomic Read and Write. A Test&Set object is a bit initially 0 whose atomic operation returns the old bit and sets it to 1; arbitrarily many initially fresh objects and registers are available. Private computation and storage are allowed. No bound on memory growth or on the number of operations in a history is imposed, but every performed step manipulates finitely represented data. No Compare&Swap, stronger atomic multi-object operation, or queue base object is supplied. Sequential queue state is a finite sequence of values from {0,1}*. Enqueue(v) appends a new occurrence of v and returns an acknowledgement. Dequeue removes and returns the first occurrence if one exists; otherwise it returns a distinguished EMPTY symbol outside the value set and leaves the queue empty. Equal values may be enqueued multiple times, but each enqueue occurrence may be removed only once. Linearizability means that each finite concurrent history can be completed by responses to some pending invocations and deletion of the others, so that its completed operations have a legal sequential FIFO order preserving each process’s order and real-time order: an operation that returns before another is invoked precedes it. Wait-freedom means that any invoked operation whose process continues taking steps returns after finitely many of that process’s own steps, regardless of other processes’ speeds or failures. No promise that another process will take a step is available. The algorithm may depend on the fixed n; the question does not require one implementation for infinitely many simultaneously participating processes. Common₂ denotes types implementable for every finite n from registers and two-process-consensus power; the cited model paper states the queue question equivalently using Test&Set. Equal consensus numbers alone do not assert mutual implementability.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct and prove correct such a deterministic implementation for every finite n, or prove impossibility for some finite n in this model. Both exact linearizability and individual wait-free progress are required. A lock-free implementation that permits starvation, a restriction on the number of enqueuers or dequeuers, duplicated removal of an occurrence, weak-empty responses, bounded histories, or a stronger atomic base type does not meet the target. An impossibility result only for strong linearizability does not rule out ordinary linearizability.

sentences: The source compares adaptive and uniform sampling for selecting the best arm after a fixed budget.
Performance is measured by the asymptotic exponential rate of recommendation error on each instance.
Two Bernoulli arms admit no strict uniform improvement over equal allocation.
For at least three Gaussian arms of common variance, a 2025 preprint proves strict improvement on every instance.

cards.definitions: An instance μ=(μ₁,…,μ_K) consists of K≥2 reward distributions with finite means θᵢ and a unique best arm i*(μ)=argmaxᵢθᵢ. At round t a policy chooses Iₜ using the known budget T, its internal randomness and previous choices and observations, then observes an independent reward from μ_{Iₜ}. After exactly T observations it recommends an arm Ĩ_T. The policy cannot depend on the unknown instance. Write p^A_{μ,T}=Pr_μ(Ĩ_T≠i*(μ)), including reward and policy randomness. The source compares H_A(μ)=limsup_{T→∞} T/log(1/p^A_{μ,T}), with smaller values better; equivalently it compares e_A(μ)=liminf_{T→∞}−T^{−1}log p^A_{μ,T}, with larger values better. Use the extended conventions 1/0=∞ and 1/∞=0. The uniform baseline used by the follow-up papers allocates approximately T/K observations to each arm with counts differing by at most one and returns an arm of largest empirical mean, breaking ties by a fixed index rule. It is not independent random allocation with fluctuating counts. The substantive domination criterion in those papers is ∀μ∈S: e_A(μ)≥e_U(μ), with strict inequality for some μ∈S. The set S, fixed before choosing the policy, is essential. The 2025 result uses S={N(θ₁,σ²),…,N(θ_K,σ²):θ has a unique maximum} for a fixed common σ²>0; the 2024 negative result uses two Bernoulli rewards with means in (0,1) and unequal means. These are distinct instance classes.
cards.answer_criterion: For a specified instance class and nontrivial domination criterion, establish one policy with the required inequality on all instances and the required strict improvement, or prove no such policy exists. An instance-specific policy that knows μ, a better finite-budget error on selected instances, or a fixed-confidence guarantee is insufficient. The already established Bernoulli and Gaussian cases must not be relabeled as open; a remaining target requires a separately justified model.

context_blocks.text: The experiment must stop after T samples. It cannot keep sampling until a chosen confidence level is reached, so fixed-confidence optimality theorems do not automatically answer this comparison.

context_blocks.title: Uniform improvement is weaker than instancewise optimality
context_blocks.text: A policy need only beat a particular baseline uniformly. It need not attain the best conceivable exponent at each instance, and impossibility of such universal optimality does not by itself rule out domination of uniform sampling.

context_blocks.title: Two Bernoulli arms give a negative answer to strict domination
context_blocks.text: The ICML 2024 theorem shows that a policy that is asymptotically no worse everywhere than equal allocation cannot strictly improve its exponent on even one instance in this class.

context_blocks.title: At least three equal-variance Gaussian arms give a positive answer
context_blocks.text: The 2025 preprint proves that certain adaptive policies have strictly larger error exponents on every unique-best-arm instance. The uniform baseline has exponent Δ_min²/(4Kσ²), where Δ_min is the difference between the largest and second-largest means.

context_blocks.title: Simple regret and error probability agree at the exponent scale

importance.reason: A proposed structural explanation for fast diameter computation across implicit geometric graphs. Existing numerical score retained.

sentences: The input is a collection of geometric objects whose intersections implicitly form a graph.
The conjecture asks whether bounded VC dimension of radius-Δ neighborhoods always permits a truly subquadratic diameter-threshold test.
Simple neighborhoods may coexist with quadratically many edges, so explicit edge enumeration is unsuitable.
The source proves that the converse is false: some fast cases have unbounded VC dimension.
The general effective object model and dependence on Δ and dimension still need to be fixed.

cards.definitions: Given n geometric objects O₁,…,O_n, their intersection graph has one vertex per object and an undirected edge ij exactly when O_i∩O_j≠∅. The input is the object descriptions, so the potentially quadratic set of edges is implicit. Graph distance dist(u,v) is the number of edges in a shortest path, and is ∞ across components. The diameter is max_{u,v}dist(u,v). Diameter-Δ asks whether it is at most the integer Δ or greater than Δ (equivalently at least Δ+1 for finite distances). Define N^Δ[v]={u:dist(u,v)≤Δ}, including v itself. A subset S of vertices is shattered by these neighborhoods if for every A⊆S there exists v with N^Δ[v]∩S=A. The VC dimension is the largest |S| that can be shattered. A constant bound must hold uniformly over growing inputs in the selected class. Bounded distance VC dimension, using all radii simultaneously, is a stronger condition than the fixed-radius version. Truly subquadratic time means O(n^{2−η}) for some fixed η>0, allowing logarithmic factors to be absorbed into a smaller positive exponent saving. Constant description complexity means a bounded number of defining parameters or predicates per object; without further restrictions it does not specify how those predicates are encoded or evaluated.
cards.answer_criterion: Fix the representation and parameter quantifiers, then prove the universal sufficient-condition algorithm or give a counterexample within that model. The time must be truly subquadratic in the number of objects, with the stated uniform exponent saving. Showing tractability for a new single shape family is progress, but does not establish the general conjecture.

context_blocks.title: Neighborhoods describe who can be reached quickly
context_blocks.text: For a fixed vertex v, N^Δ[v] records all objects reachable from it in at most Δ intersections. Bounded VC dimension says these reachable sets cannot realize every pattern on a large collection of test vertices. It limits their combinatorial variety, rather than their sizes.

context_blocks.title: Even a dense graph can have simple neighborhoods
context_blocks.text: If all objects intersect one another, the graph is complete and every radius-1 neighborhood is the whole vertex set. Its VC dimension is zero, although the graph has Θ(n²) edges. This is why the algorithm must work from object descriptions rather than enumerate all edges.

context_blocks.title: The conjecture is only a sufficient condition
context_blocks.text: The paper gives a subquadratic Diameter-2 algorithm for boxes despite unbounded relevant VC dimension. Thus unbounded VC dimension does not by itself imply hardness, and an “if and only if” reformulation would contradict a result in the source.

context_blocks.title: Existing bounded-VC algorithms do not cover every implicit graph
context_blocks.text: A related framework has time depending on the edge count m for general sparse graphs, alongside stronger results for specific geometric families. Substituting m=Θ(n²) does not produce the desired O(n^{2−η}) guarantee. The extra geometric input structure remains relevant.

context_blocks.title: Disks provide a concrete unresolved test case
context_blocks.text: The source highlights ordinary disks of varying radii in the plane: their intersection graphs have bounded distance VC dimension, but the paper does not know a truly subquadratic Diameter-2 algorithm for them. This is distinct from the already solved unit-disk case.

notes: Recovered the complete source question and identified its remaining model choices.
statement_review.remaining_issue: The source defines low complexity only as constant description complexity. A universal algorithmic statement still needs a specified effective representation/object class and computation model, a convention for whether Δ is fixed or part of the input, and the permitted dependence of the exponent on Δ, ambient dimension and the VC bound. The geometric input must remain implicit; an explicit adjacency matrix would already cost Θ(n²) to read. Choosing a particular semialgebraic representation or a fixed Δ would specialize the source conjecture and is not done silently.

changes: Recovered Conjecture 8 and defined shattering, closed neighborhoods and the implicit graph model.
Separated sufficient from necessary conditions and dense from sparse graph bounds.
Recorded the missing universal representation and parameter conventions.
quality_review.scope: Checked the statement, model, answer criterion, context, significance and cited results; searched for subsequent work. Searches are not exhaustive, and paper proofs were not independently verified.

cards.context:
For a fixed vertex v, N^Δ[v] records all objects reachable from it in at most Δ intersections. Bounded VC dimension says these reachable sets cannot realize every pattern on a large collection of test vertices. It limits their combinatorial variety, rather than their sizes.

If all objects intersect one another, the graph is complete and every radius-1 neighborhood is the whole vertex set. Its VC dimension is zero, although the graph has Θ(n²) edges. This is why the algorithm must work from object descriptions rather than enumerate all edges.

The paper gives a subquadratic Diameter-2 algorithm for boxes despite unbounded relevant VC dimension. Thus unbounded VC dimension does not by itself imply hardness, and an “if and only if” reformulation would contradict a result in the source.

A related framework has time depending on the edge count m for general sparse graphs, alongside stronger results for specific geometric families. Substituting m=Θ(n²) does not produce the desired O(n^{2−η}) guarantee. The extra geometric input structure remains relevant.

The source highlights ordinary disks of varying radii in the plane: their intersection graphs have bounded distance VC dimension, but the paper does not know a truly subquadratic Diameter-2 algorithm for them. This is distinct from the already solved unit-disk case.

cards.title: Local regularization for multiclass learning
cards.formal: Does every realizably PAC-learnable multiclass hypothesis class H admit a fixed local regularizer ψ:H×X→ℝ≥0 such that every learner induced by ψ, under the pointwise minimum-score rule below, PAC learns H? cards.why: Tests whether a fixed preference over hypotheses at each prediction point is a general principle for multiclass learning. cards.definitions: Let X be an instance space, Y a label space that may be infinite, and H⊆Y^X a nonempty class of predictors h:X→Y. A distribution D on labeled examples X×Y is realizable by H if some h*∈H satisfies PrD[h*(x)≠y]=0. The risk of a predictor g is LD(g)=PrD[g(x)≠y]. A learner A maps a finite labeled sample S to a predictor A(S), which need not belong to H. It PAC learns H if, for every ε,δ∈(0,1), there is mA(ε,δ)<∞ such that for every H-realizable D and every m≥mA(ε,δ), a sample S of m independent draws from D satisfies Pr[LD(A(S))>ε]≤δ. Probability spaces, predictors and learners are understood with measurable error events, so these probabilities are defined. There is no running-time requirement. For a nonempty realizable sample S, the version space H[S] consists of all h∈H agreeing with every labeled example in S. A local regularizer assigns each pair (h,x) a nonnegative real score ψ(h,x), fixed before observing S. It is admissible only if a minimum score on H[S] is attained at every test point x and the induced prediction rules are well-defined; an empty argmin cannot make the claim vacuously true. A learner is induced by ψ when A(S)(x) belongs to {h(x): h∈argmin g∈H[S] ψ(g,x)} for every such S,x. On empty or unrealizable samples its behavior is unrestricted. The quantifier “every induced learner” includes every valid tie-breaking rule; its sample bound may depend on that learner. The regularizer can depend on H and x, but not on S, its size, its unlabeled points, D, ε or δ.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every realizably PAC-learnable H has such an admissible regularizer, or give a PAC-learnable class H and prove that every admissible local regularizer induces at least one learner that is not PAC consistent in the stated distribution-independent sense. A favorable tie-breaking rule alone is insufficient. Neither a transductive separation nor failure of proper learning alone settles this PAC question.

context_blocks.title: A different preference at each test point
context_blocks.text: A regularizer expresses which hypotheses the learning rule prefers. Local regularization lets that preference depend on the new point being classified. After training, only hypotheses that fit the sample remain eligible, and the rule predicts using a least-scored eligible hypothesis at that point.

context_blocks.title: Why the prediction can be outside the class
context_blocks.text: One hypothesis might be preferred in one region of X and another in a different region. The resulting predictor can combine their labels without being a single hypothesis from H. This flexibility matters because some multiclass problems are learnable only by allowing such improper output.

context_blocks.title: Ties carry a real quantifier
context_blocks.text: The source asks the regularizer to succeed for every induced tie-breaking learner. If all scores are zero, the rule imposes no preference among sample-consistent hypotheses. Selecting one specially chosen successful learner from those ties would not show that the regularizer itself learns the class. Likewise, score minima must exist for the prediction rule to be meaningful.

context_blocks.title: Sample-dependent regularization is a different model
context_blocks.text: The source reports a general positive result when a local regularizer may first use the unlabeled training points. Here the score function is fixed independently of the sample. The question tests whether that extra sample information is necessary for a general multiclass learning rule.

context_blocks.title: Two 2026 claims of a negative resolution
context_blocks.text: Hou’s July preprint claims a countable learnable class beyond all local regularizers. The August preprint by Asilis and coauthors independently claims a PAC counterexample under the same worst-case tie convention and acknowledges Hou’s work. The checked statements match the main question, but their full lower-bound proofs have not been independently verified in this review. The card therefore records a claimed negative resolution with uncertain status.

cards.definitions: A concept class C_n is a nonempty set of functions X_n→{0,1}, with a fixed common input and hypothesis representation in both models. Data consist of independent examples (x,f*(x)), where x follows an unknown distribution P on X_n and f*:X_n→{0,1} is an arbitrary fixed labeling function, not necessarily in C_n. A membership query chooses any x∈X_n and receives f*(x); repeated queries have the same label. For h∈C_n, define err_P(h)=Pr_{x∼P}[h(x)≠f*(x)] and opt=inf_{g∈C_n}err_P(g). Given accuracy ε and failure probability δ, a testable learner returns h∈C_n or the rejection symbol ⊥. Soundness holds for every P and f*: Pr[h≠⊥ and err_P(h)>opt+ε]≤δ. Completeness holds whenever P=D_n: Pr[h=⊥]≤δ. Probabilities are over samples and the learner’s randomness. This explicitly uses the usual joint bad-output event for the source’s informal “if it outputs” guarantee, not conditioning on a potentially extremely rare acceptance event. The sample-only learner has no membership oracle and satisfies the same two guarantees. Running time includes sample/query processing and writing the hypothesis; encodings and any given target-distribution description are unchanged. Polynomial overhead is understood in the standard parameterized sense, accounting for input size, 1/ε and log(1/δ) as well as the query learner’s time. The agnostic coefficient on opt is exactly one; an unspecified constant multiple is the different semi-agnostic model.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication by constructing sample-only testable learners with polynomially related resource bounds and the same agnostic guarantee, or exhibit a class/distribution family with a superpolynomial separation between the two testable-learning access models. Reducing query-based testable learning merely to ordinary sample-based agnostic learning is insufficient, because ordinary learning lacks soundness outside the target distribution.

cards.definitions: Arithmetic in 𝔽₂={0,1} uses addition and multiplication modulo two; ⟨a,x⟩=Σᵢ₌₁ⁿaᵢxᵢ mod 2. First choose x uniformly from {0,1}^n and hold it fixed. Independently for each t, choose a_t uniformly from {0,1}^n and a noise bit Z_t with Pr[Z_t=1]=1/2−ε; observe (a_t,b_t) with b_t=⟨a_t,x⟩+Z_t mod 2. Noise bits, query vectors and internal learner coins are mutually independent. The learner outputs one estimate x̂; success means x̂=x, and its probability averages over x, all observations and internal coins. The learner sees each sample once in order, cannot choose a_t or revisit discarded observations, and has no computational-time restriction. Formally use a branching program with T+1 layers and width at most 2^S, one start vertex and one outgoing edge for each possible sample at each nonterminal vertex, all going to the next layer. Leaves, possibly in earlier layers, are labelled by estimates in {0,1}^n. Randomized learners may use fresh coins to choose state updates; retained coins are part of the state. Equivalently, the lower bound may be checked on deterministic nonuniform programs, since a random tape can be fixed to achieve at least the average success under this fixed input distribution without increasing width or length. The program may depend on n and ε; its transition description, current layer and input sample are not charged as stored data. Memory counts persistent state bits, S=⌈log₂(width)⌉, and T is the maximum number of consumed samples, not its expectation. No hypothesis is made about the hardness of LPN in unrestricted computation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal bounded-error memory/sample tradeoff with constants uniform in ε, or refute that asymptotic claim by showing that no such constants can work. A bound Ω(n²/ε), a result only for constant ε, or a lower bound in a restricted statistical-query model does not settle the proposed dependence on noise.

Without noise, every observation is a correct linear relation about the hidden vector. Here the relation is only slightly more likely to be right than wrong when ε is small. The question asks whether this forces a quadratic loss in the storage threshold as the bias tends to zero.

The source proves that a learner needs Ω(n²/ε) memory or exponentially many samples, and records an upper bound using O(n²/ε²) memory and O(n/ε²) samples. The conjecture asks whether the stronger memory dependence is necessary below an exponential sample budget.

The lower bound concerns retained information, not the time needed to process it. It must hold for arbitrary state-transition rules and therefore would be unconditional even though efficient learning of noisy parity is also used as a computational hardness assumption.

For ε fixed away from zero, the two memory bounds differ only by constants. The unresolved content is their uniform dependence on ε, together with an exponential sample threshold whose exponent does not shrink with ε.

The 2024 DIMACS project abstract identifies the same n²/ε²-versus-exponential tradeoff as its long-term goal and describes intermediate observations in a modified model. It is evidence of continued study, not a proved lower bound or a fresh claim that all later work has been exhausted.

cards.definitions: R(σ) permutes the tensor factors labelled by X: R(σ)|a⟩=|a∘σ⁻¹⟩ for a∈{0,1}^X. A finite abstract group acting on X is represented by its image in Sym(X); only this action matters. Circuit wires are W=X⊔Y, with X active and Y workspace. Allowed gates are arbitrary one-qubit unitaries and unbounded-fan-in reversible threshold/equality gates. For S⊆W, target h∉S and integer t≥0, a threshold gate flips bit a_h exactly when ∑_{s∈S}a_s≥t; an equality gate flips it exactly when this sum equals t, leaving all other bits unchanged and extending linearly to quantum states. Layers are sets of pairwise commuting gates; gates within a layer may share wires. A wire permutation acts on a gate by relabelling its target and controls while preserving the one-qubit matrix or threshold value. The circuit is Γ-symmetric if, for each σ∈Γ, some permutation π of W restricts to σ on X and maps each layer to itself as a set of labelled gates. The extensions π need not be selected as a group homomorphism. This is a syntactic circuit condition, stronger than merely requiring its resulting unitary to commute with Γ. Implementation is exact on the full active Hilbert space, with clean workspace, no intermediate measurements or postselection, and no uniformity or finite-angle-encoding restriction on the arbitrary one-qubit gates. An overall input-independent phase can be absorbed into an allowed one-qubit phase gate.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove exact implementability for every finite permutation action and every commuting unitary, or exhibit an action and a commuting unitary that no finite circuit in this model implements. A lower bound only on polynomial-size circuits does not refute universality. Implementing only the invariant-state subspace does not implement an arbitrary unitary on the whole space.

context_blocks.title: Symmetry must be visible throughout the circuit
context_blocks.text: Suppose Γ swaps two active wires. Applying the same one-qubit gate to both wires in a common layer respects that swap. Applying different gates to the two wires generally does not. More elaborate circuits may use extra wires, but every active-wire symmetry must still extend to a relabelling that preserves every layer.

context_blocks.title: Workspace can transform under the symmetry
context_blocks.text: Ancillas are not required to be fixed individually. A swap of active wires may also swap corresponding workspace wires. They begin and end at zero, so they can support a symmetric computation without supplying an asymmetric initial resource.

context_blocks.title: A substantial family of groups is already understood

This includes the full permutation group S_n. The remaining question allows other finite actions, such as a cyclic rotation of wire labels.

context_blocks.title: Full-space universality differs from efficient subspace implementation

cards.definitions: A positional proof places verifiers and honest provers at points p(Q) of a metric space (X,d). A message emitted at time t cannot reach another point before its distance-dependent arrival time. In the formal model, time is discrete, d is integer-valued, the timeout and verifier computation are polynomial in the input length, and quantum messages are passed through local completely positive trace-preserving operations. Malicious strategies may change prover locations while keeping verifier locations fixed and must obey the specified routing and timing constraints. A verifier’s min-ball is B_V={z:d(z,p(V))≤min_P d(p(P),p(V))}. The min-ball condition holds when two such balls are disjoint. In the geometric pyramid illustration, k verifiers lie on a regular k-gon of circumradius R in the plane z=0, another verifier lies at height √(4r²−R²) for r>R, and each of k honest provers lies at the midpoint between a polygon verifier and the top verifier. The balls pairwise intersect but have no common point. PSPACE is the class of languages decidable by deterministic polynomial-space machines; EXP allows deterministic time 2^{poly(n)}. The source’s superscript s means separable initial prover resources and its associated no-PE transmission rules. Arbitrary prior entanglement would permit a joint quantum state across malicious prover locations before verifier challenges, with no fixed finite bound on its dimension; this is a change to the soundness model, not a theorem about the original no-PE class.
cards.answer_criterion: Precisely define the entangled-adversary variant and prove that every language with a proof in that class lies in PSPACE, with the claimed lower inclusion if stating equality; or establish a counterexample under explicitly stated complexity assumptions. Demonstrating failure of the source’s particular EXP construction establishes an attack on that protocol, not a collapse of all protocols for the arrangement.

cards.definitions: A promise problem is a pair (L_yes,L_no) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings, with no required answer outside their union. Membership in StoqMA(a,b) means there is a deterministic polynomial-time procedure which, given x of length n, produces a verification circuit V_x on m(n)+r(n)+s(n) qubits, all counts polynomially bounded in n. Its initial state is |w⟩⊗|0⟩^{⊗r}⊗|+⟩^{⊗s}, where |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and the m-qubit witness has norm one. The circuit uses only classical reversible gates: NOT flips a bit, CNOT flips its target if its control is one, and Toffoli flips its target if both controls are one. These gates act linearly on computational-basis states. There are no intermediate measurements or arbitrary quantum gates. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the {|+⟩,|−⟩} basis, with |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2, and outcome + means acceptance. Its acceptance probability is the squared norm after projection onto |+⟩ on that qubit. If x∈L_yes, some witness with real nonnegative computational-basis amplitudes must be accepted with probability at least a(n). If x∈L_no, every normalized witness, including arbitrary complex amplitudes, must be accepted with probability at most b(n). The source proves that a maximizing witness can be chosen nonnegative. Efficient threshold computability is understood in the standard precision sense: their values can be approximated within 2^{−t} in time polynomial in n+t. The inverse-polynomial gap permits this conventional representation. Class containment quantifies over promise problems and asserts existence of new uniform verifiers; it does not demand a blackbox compiler acting on an arbitrary verifier description. Polynomial bounds of the new verifier may depend on the original verifier, q and ℓ. Soundness approaches 1/2 from above, not zero; the requested improvement is relative to the stoquastic acceptance baseline.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the containment for every admissible a,b and ℓ, or refute this universally quantified amplification statement. A positive answer must achieve both exponentially small completeness error and exponentially small excess soundness above 1/2 while retaining the allowed gates, initial ancillas and final measurement. Soundness-only repetition, perfect-completeness special cases, extra destructive-interference gates, or additional unentangled provers do not establish the claim.

context_blocks.title: The verifier has a restricted way to accept
context_blocks.text: The computation is classically reversible, but its ancillas and final measurement allow a nonnegative quantum witness to affect acceptance. This restricted verification model arises in the complexity of stoquastic local Hamiltonians. Familiar error-reduction statements for unrestricted quantum verification do not automatically give the required stoquastic verifier.

context_blocks.title: Soundness reduction alone is known
context_blocks.text: The source’s Theorem 5 maps thresholds (1/2+u/2,1/2+v/2) to (1/2+u^r/2,1/2+v^r/2) for polynomial r. This improves excess soundness but can also lower completeness. Conjecture 6 asks for simultaneous amplification towards completeness one and soundness one half.

context_blocks.title: Amplification would identify StoqMA with MA
context_blocks.text: The 2025 published paper proves that negligible completeness error with a suitable inverse-polynomial gap is already contained in MA, the class of promise problems verified in polynomial time with a classical witness and random bits. Its Corollary 1.5 makes general StoqMA error reduction equivalent to StoqMA=MA.

context_blocks.title: Recent multiwitness work keeps the question open
context_blocks.text: The July 2026 preprint still explicitly calls general one-witness error reduction open. Its restricted repetition results do not supply the two threshold limits required here for arbitrary original completeness.

context_blocks.title: Prover collapse is a separate claim
context_blocks.text: The May 2026 preprint claims that the number of stoquastic provers can be reduced while retaining an inverse-polynomial gap. It explicitly avoids assuming general amplification. This preprint claim is not recorded as a solution of the one-witness error-reduction question.

cards.definitions: A Boolean CNF is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals. Over a fixed field K, encode each clause by the product of the factors that equal one when its literals are false, set that product to zero, and add x_i²−x_i=0 for Boolean variables. For example, x∨¬y becomes (1−x)y=0. Let f_1(x),…,f_m(x) be the resulting polynomials. An IPS certificate is a polynomial C(x,y) with C(x,0)=0 and C(x,f_1(x),…,f_m(x))=1 as polynomial identities; an IPS refutation is an arithmetic circuit over K computing C. A group Γ acts by permutations of the x variables and preserves the polynomial axiom set; it then permutes y_i according to the induced permutation of f_i. The circuit is Γ-symmetric when each group permutation extends to a permutation of its gates preserving wires, operation labels and field constants. Polynomial invariance of its output alone is weaker than this circuit requirement. Size is measured by circuit gates with the instance-size floor; a superpolynomial family lower bound excludes any one polynomial bound in encoded formula size. In the ordinary nonsymmetric setting, VP consists of polynomial-degree polynomial families in polynomially many variables having polynomial-size arithmetic circuits. VNP consists of families expressible as a sum over polynomially many Boolean witness variables of such a VP family. How to impose compatible symmetries on these families and on the summation is a missing part of the proposed analogue.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify and justify the symmetric algebraic classes and compatible CNF/group families, then prove or refute the stated implication under those fixed definitions. A lower bound for invariant polynomials, for a bounded-degree IPS fragment, or only for Hilbert-like certificates does not automatically establish a lower bound for the full symmetric IPS system.

cards.definitions: A literal is xᵢ or its negation ¬xᵢ. A clause is a disjunction of literals and a CNF F is a finite conjunction of clauses over variables x₁,…,xₙ; unsatisfiable means no Boolean assignment satisfies every clause. Resolution derives C∨D from C∨xᵢ and D∨¬xᵢ, and allows weakening from C to C∨D; input clauses can be used as axioms. A refutation derives the empty clause. A tree-like proof uses each derived occurrence as a premise at most once, duplicating occurrences when necessary; S_T(F) is the minimum number of leaves, rather than total literal count. A configuration proof starts with no stored clauses and at each step downloads an input clause, erases a stored clause, or adds a resolvent/weakening of clauses currently stored; it ends with the empty clause stored. CSpace(F) is the minimum, over such proofs with unrestricted length, of the maximum number of simultaneously stored clauses. For PCR fix K and use the polynomial ring K[x₁,…,xₙ,y₁,…,yₙ], where yᵢ represents ¬xᵢ. A line P means P=0. Logical axioms are z²−z for each z among xᵢ,yᵢ and xᵢ+yᵢ−1. The encoding of a clause is the product of its false-literal indicators: xᵢ contributes yᵢ and ¬xᵢ contributes xᵢ. From P,Q derive αP+βQ for α,β∈K; from P derive zP for any literal variable z. A PCR refutation derives 1. Its configurations may download axioms, erase lines or add an inference whose premises are stored. The monomial space of a configuration is the number of distinct formal monomials with nonzero coefficients occurring anywhere in its stored polynomials, counted once across all lines; coefficients and exponents are not separately charged. MSpace_K(F) is the minimum maximum monomial space over all PCR refutations. Every proof is finite and minima concern the specified syntactic systems. The source’s relation A⪯B permits A(F)≤((B(F))log n)^{O(1)}; ≈ means both directions. The harmless +1 terms here cover one-leaf or other constant-size cases. No polynomial-length restriction is imposed on the space-minimizing proof.
cards.answer_criterion: For each stated space measure, prove the universal polynomial/logarithmic simulation bound or refute it by showing that no constants C,a work for all unsatisfiable formulas (with K fixed in the PCR case). The two variants must be reported separately. A polynomial separation between raw measures does not refute a comparison that explicitly permits arbitrary polynomial and logarithmic factors.

references.authors: Hatami, Hamed; Hatami, Pooya; Pires, William; Tao, Ran; Zhao, Rosie
references.locator: Question 1.4; PDF page 3

cards.definitions: A sign matrix A∈{−1,+1}^{r×s} has positive finite numbers r,s of rows and columns and has every entry specified. Its sign-rank rank±(A) is the least D≥1 for which there are unit vectors u₁,…,uᵣ,v₁,…,vₛ∈ℝᴰ with Aᵢⱼ⟨uᵢ,vⱼ⟩>0 for all i,j. Equivalently it is the minimum real rank of a matrix B satisfying AᵢⱼBᵢⱼ>0 entrywise; zero entries do not realize either sign. The margin m(A) is the supremum, over such unit-vector representations in all finite dimensions D, of min_{i,j} Aᵢⱼ⟨uᵢ,vⱼ⟩. It lies in (0,1]. In optimizing margin, the representation dimension is unrestricted; the representation of least dimension need not maximize margin. The requested d may grow arbitrarily rapidly as ρ tends to zero, but for each fixed positive ρ it must bound all matrix sizes. Equivalently, one can use a finite nondecreasing bounding function η:[1,∞)→ℕ. This uniform bounded-margin interpretation is explicitly restated in the later source’s Open Problem 1.3. Matrices with missing or promise-restricted entries are excluded.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a finite size-independent bound d(ρ) for every positive margin threshold ρ, or prove there is a fixed ρ>0 and a sequence of fully specified finite sign matrices with margins at least ρ and unbounded sign-ranks. No efficient procedure for producing the low-dimensional representation is required. Unbounded sign-rank with margins tending to zero, or only for partial matrices, does not refute the statement.

cards.definitions: γₙ is standard Gaussian probability measure, the law of X with independent N(0,1) coordinates. Central symmetry means K=−K, with symmetry about the origin. Convexity means tx+(1−t)y∈K for x,y∈K and t∈[0,1]. Write 1_K for the indicator of K. The convex influence in a Euclidean unit direction v is Inf_v[K]=(1/√2) E[1_K(X)(1−⟨v,X⟩²)]. This is nonnegative for centrally symmetric convex K. The orthogonal subspace is v⊥={y:⟨v,y⟩=0}, and C+ℝv={y+tv:y∈C,t∈ℝ} is a cylinder whose membership depends only on the projection x−⟨v,x⟩v. The symmetric difference K△L consists of points in exactly one of K and L, so its Gaussian measure is the probability that their membership indicators disagree. Empty sets and the whole space are permitted. No lower or upper bound away from zero or one is imposed on γₙ(K), and no bound on total influence is assumed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a single modulus τ tending to zero that bounds the Gaussian approximation error uniformly over the stated sets, dimensions and directions, or prove that no such modulus exists. Equivalently for a negative answer, exhibit a sequence with directional influence tending to zero while its Gaussian distance from every symmetric convex cylinder in that direction stays bounded below by a positive constant. A dimension-dependent modulus or a cylinder in some other direction does not suffice.

references.authors: Chakraborty, Sourav; Mande, Nikhil S.; Mittal, Rajat; Molli, Tulasimohan; Paraashar, Manaswi; Sanyal, Swagato
